Content covers: the mishnah's daily-offering priest counts (nine on weekdays, growing to eleven on festivals for the two libations, twelve when festival Shabbat adds the two-log arrangement); the Gemara's derivation from 'and the priest shall kindle it' (singular, morning) versus 'and they shall arrange' (plural, twice, afternoon) that only the afternoon tamid needs two priests carrying two logs; the mishnah's instruction to the one pouring the water libation to raise his hand, and the story of the Sadducee priest who poured the water on his feet instead of the altar bowl in rejection of the Oral Law's water-libation ruling, tied to the 'with their citrons' phrase limiting the libation's occasion to Sukkot; the Gemara's proof from the singular/plural verse pair that the wood arrangement must use two priests specifically in the afternoon, not the morning; the extended sometimes-thirteen-through-sometimes-seventeen priest-count sequence explaining each increment (regular daily service, the added festival water flask, Shabbat's wood addition, Shabbat-within-festival compounding both), closing on the seventeen-priest baraita variant that Rashi reconciles with Rabbi Yehuda's position (no fire-pan lottery, but a priest for ramp-to-altar carrying) rather than Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's, including Rashi's own transmission-uncertainty caveat about the exact wording he received; and the opening of the next mishnah on flesh/fine-flour priest counts and the case of a priest who wishes to offer his own portion alone without a lottery, closing on the question (continuing to 27a) of whether a non-priest may validly perform flaying and dismemberment.
